query: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges? Specify a controlled comparison that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the initial baseline, its service and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.

generation.hypothesis: In single-phase high-entropy alloys with nominally stable solid-solution microstructures, brittle fracture can emerge because minor segregation and short-range ordering near grain boundaries progressively reduce local cohesion under mechanical and thermal stresses, leading to intergranular or transgranular crack initiation and propagation.
generation.material_initial_state: A homogenized (solution-treated) single-phase high-entropy alloy (e.g., CoCrFeMnNi) with uniform equiaxed grains and minimal second-phase precipitates, suitable for use in demanding engineering conditions.
generation.intervention: Correlative in-situ electron microscopy and spectroscopy during small-scale mechanical loading at service-relevant temperatures, combined with controlled additions of trace solute elements and varied aging treatments to induce grain-boundary compositional fluctuations or short-range order.
generation.conditions: Mechanical tests over a range of temperatures (e.g., room temperature to 800 °C) and strain rates (e.g., 10−4 s−1 to 10−1 s−1), with carefully introduced minor-element doping levels and controlled time–temperature exposures, to track the onset of embrittlement.
generation.structural_mediator: Local grain-boundary environment enriched in specific solute elements or short-range ordered clusters that undermine boundary cohesion or disrupt dislocationmediated plastic flow.
generation.mechanism: As minor segregation accumulates or short-range ordering develops at grain boundaries under stress and high or cryogenic temperatures, boundary cohesion diminishes, allowing microcracks to initiate and propagate more readily, leading to reduced toughness.
generation.predicted_outcome: A shift from ductile to partially brittle fracture after prolonged boundary segregation or short-range ordering, manifested by reduced fracture toughness and the appearance of intergranular or cleavage-like crack morphologies compared to the initially ductile baseline.
generation.baseline: Solution-treated high-entropy alloy with minimal grain-boundary segregation or ordering shows a relatively high toughness and ductile failure behavior.
generation.boundary: Under prolonged aging or at extremes of temperature (either relatively high or cryogenic) that promote segregation or ordering, the alloy transitions to quasi-brittle fracture; beyond a threshold of local boundary changes, brittle failure becomes predominant.
generation.uncertainty: Exact solute segregation levels, temperature thresholds, and time scales for the onset of brittle boundaries remain insufficiently constrained by existing studies.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct in-situ STEM/EELS to measure boundary composition during incremental dwell times at elevated temperatures and simultaneously perform micro-pillaring or nanoindentation at boundary regions in a TEM to observe crack initiation. Compare doping variations and reference conditions to test whether increasing segregation or short-range ordering precedes brittle boundary failure.
measurements: Spatially resolved chemical composition at grain boundaries via EELS or EDX
Real-time crack initiation and propagation observation through TEM imaging under load
Fracture toughness measurements before and after aging or doping
Quantitative correlation of boundary composition with local hardness/toughness
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If boundary chemical fluctuations do not precede or accompany the onset of brittle fracture (i.e., no identifiable segregation or ordering is observed at boundaries, yet embrittlement still occurs), or if increasing solute fluctuations do not correlate with transitions to brittle fracture, the hypothesis is invalidated.

decision.trend: Early studies (PMC4740901) established that single-phase CrCoNi alloys can exhibit exceptional toughness, especially at cryogenic temperatures, revealing a marked capacity for stable plastic deformation. Subsequent work (PMC5461481) showed that the prototype CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloy maintains a single-phase fcc structure, though it can undergo pressure-induced transformations to hcp, suggesting possible phase instability pathways. Later investigations on a refractory BCC high-entropy alloy (PMC11206460) demonstrated strong retention of mechanical properties at high temperatures but did not fully address potential grain-boundary embrittlement. More recent efforts (PMC11330973) explored a lightweight single-phase Al-based complex concentrated alloy with very high specific strength, yet the role of local chemical fluctuations and boundary phenomena in affecting toughness at both low and elevated temperatures remains unclear.
decision.unsolved: Despite evidence of robust damage tolerance in single-phase high-entropy alloys, it is not yet established how local segregation, short-range ordering, or nanoscale precipitates at boundaries might trigger embrittlement under demanding service conditions. The precise linkage between these potential microstructural changes and evolving fracture behavior remains an open question.
decision.lever: Correlative in-situ electron microscopy, spectroscopy, and small-scale mechanical testing at service-relevant temperatures, focusing on real-time monitoring of boundary regions and local chemical changes during loading.
decision.why: This approach directly addresses whether grain-boundary segregation or phase fluctuations initiate brittle failure in single-phase high-entropy alloys under the thermal and mechanical stresses of engineering applications, providing the mechanistic insights needed to distinguish their behavior from conventional alloys and to falsify hypothesized embrittlement pathways.
